author: opus-builder
question: Is TypeScript catching up with JavaScript on GitHub?
title: Is TypeScript catching up with JavaScript on GitHub?

licenceStatements.quote: The dataset is made available under a CC0-1.0 license.

upstream.indicator: num_pushers by language, economy and quarter (languages.csv)
upstream.source: GitHub (first-party aggregate of public platform activity; no third-party input)

definitions.num_pushers: the number of unique developers in each economy who made at least one git push to a repository with a given programming language during each quarter (datasheet l.37)
definitions.threshold: Metrics for economies are only reported when there are 100 or more unique developers performing the relevant activity within the time period (datasheet l.25 and l.120)
definitions.location: assigned by the developer's IP address, the mode of daily samples in the quarter (datasheet l.27)

params.excludeReason: EU is an aggregate reported beside its member states (DATASETS.md B6); counting it would count those developers twice.

promise.answerSentence: As a share of JavaScript, yes, and quickly; in raw numbers, no: JavaScript's lead grew.
promise.why: G5 RC1/RC5 (audits/t1-promise.json): both halves of the answer inside the first 30 seconds.

octoverse_2025.title: Octoverse: A new developer joins GitHub every second as AI leads TypeScript to #1
octoverse_2025.quote: By GitHub contributor counts, August 2025 marks the first time TypeScript emerged as the most used language on GitHub
octoverse_2025.sentence: GitHub's Octoverse 2025 report named TypeScript the most used language on GitHub in August 2025, by contributor counts.

supporting.quote: languages are ranked by the number of distinct monthly contributors who committed code in that language
supporting.supports: How Octoverse counts: monthly contributors who committed code in a language. With datasheet l.37 (quarterly developers who pushed to a repository containing the language) it backs 'That is a different count from the quarterly pushers in this video.'

octoverse_2025.note: Attributed statement, not a figure: nothing in it is computed from the dataset. Its one number, the year, is the only exception to the no-hand-typed-numbers rule (sources.py). Octoverse also gives JavaScript 2.15M contributors (l.682); the narration does not use it.

citations.quote: The files and directories within a repository determine the languages that make up the repository.
citations.supports: RC3: 'a repository that holds both languages counts for both'

citations.quote: who made at least one git push to a repository with a given programming language during each quarter
citations.supports: RC3 and the s1 counting sentence: the count is developers pushing to a repository with (containing) the language

citations.quote: languages are ranked by the number of distinct monthly contributors who committed code in that language
citations.supports: 'That is a different count from the quarterly pushers in this video.'

page.note: The web page carries the brand. The video carries no brand name (render.py refuses one in the title, description or script).

scenes.chartTitle: Developers who pushed to repositories containing TypeScript or JavaScript
scenes.alt: Line chart of developers pushing to repositories containing TypeScript and to repositories containing JavaScript each quarter, summed over the {fig:panel_economies} economies reported for both languages in every quarter from {fig:first_quarter} to {fig:last_quarter}.
scenes.narration: Is TypeScript catching up with JavaScript on GitHub? As a share of JavaScript, yes, and quickly; in raw numbers, no: JavaScript's lead grew. Every quarter, GitHub counts the developers in each economy who push to repositories containing each language; a repository that holds both languages counts for both. We follow the {fig:panel_economies} economies reported for both in every quarter.

scenes.chartTitle: TypeScript pushers as a share of JavaScript pushers
scenes.alt: Line chart of TypeScript pushers as a percentage of JavaScript pushers, rising from {fig:ratio_first_pct} in {fig:first_quarter} to {fig:ratio_last_pct} in {fig:last_quarter}.
scenes.narration: In {fig:first_quarter}, TypeScript had {fig:ratio_first_pct} as many pushers as JavaScript. By {fig:last_quarter}, it had {fig:ratio_last_pct}. In raw numbers, though, JavaScript's lead grew, from {fig:gap_first_millions} to {fig:gap_last_millions} pushers, because both languages grew. {src:octoverse_2025} That is a different count from the quarterly pushers in this video.

scenes.chartTitle: How many times over each language's pushers grew
scenes.alt: Bar chart of the growth multiple of pushers for the {fig:top_n} languages with the most pushers in {fig:last_quarter}; {fig:fastest_top_language} grew fastest, {fig:a_growth_x} over.
scenes.narration: Over the {fig:span_years} years, TypeScript pushers grew {fig:a_growth_x} over, and JavaScript pushers {fig:b_growth_x}. Among the {fig:top_n} languages with the most pushers, the fastest growing was {fig:fastest_top_language}.

scenes.chartTitle: Year-on-year change in the TypeScript-to-JavaScript ratio
scenes.alt: Bar chart of the yearly change in the TypeScript-to-JavaScript ratio; the last year's rise of {fig:ratio_gain_last_pts} is the largest, against at most {fig:ratio_gain_max_earlier_pts} in earlier years.
scenes.narration: The ratio moved fastest in the last year: it rose {fig:ratio_gain_last_pts}, against at most {fig:ratio_gain_max_earlier_pts} in any earlier year.

scenes.chartTitle: The TypeScript-to-JavaScript ratio, economy by economy
scenes.alt: Histogram of the TypeScript-to-JavaScript ratio across the {fig:panel_economies} economies in {fig:first_quarter} and in {fig:last_quarter}; {fig:econ_at_threshold_last} economies are at {fig:threshold_pct} or more in the later quarter.
scenes.narration: Economy by economy, the picture is the same. TypeScript reached {fig:threshold_pct} of JavaScript's pushers in {fig:econ_at_threshold_last} of the {fig:panel_economies} economies, up from {fig:econ_at_threshold_first} in {fig:first_year}. The highest ratio was {fig:max_ratio_last_pct}.

scenes.alt: Line chart of how many economies GitHub reports each quarter for TypeScript and for JavaScript; for TypeScript it rose from {fig:econ_reported_a_first} to {fig:econ_reported_a_last}.
scenes.narration: Limits: GitHub omits economies with too few active developers; those reported for TypeScript rose from {fig:econ_reported_a_first} to {fig:econ_reported_a_last}, hence the fixed set. Only public repositories count, developers can count under both, and location comes from IP addresses. The data shows how many pushed, not why. Source: GitHub's Innovation Graph, public domain.
